newsitem.title: USA: Republicans fear opportunity in Texas slipping away.
newsitem.headline: Republicans fear opportunity in Texas slipping away.

text.p: The Democrats' glory days in Texas are long gone but Republican leaders fear a golden opportunity to win a historic shift in the balance of power in its congressional delegation is slipping away.

Their frustration is all the more acute because control of the U.S. House could easily hang on special elections in a handful of Texas districts where the boundaries have been redrawn in a dispute over gerrymandering.

Just two months ago, Republicans were confident of gaining at least four House seats in Texas, giving them control of its 30-member congressional delegation for the first time and dealing a possibly fatal setback to all-out nationwide Democratic drive to regain a House majority.

Now that confidence has largely evaporated and party leaders say they need Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole to surge in the polls if they are to have a chance of toppling more Democrats here.
"I'm just not happy with the situation. It's a lot tighter in Texas than it ought to be," said Tom Pauken, chairman of the state Republican Party. "We could win two or lose two."
Pauken and others put the problem down to President Bill Clinton's political resurgence and Dole's lackluster campaign.
"In 1994, Bill Clinton couldn't have got 35 percent of the vote in Texas and now he is running a competitive race here. So something has gone wrong," Pauken said.

Royal Masset, Republican Party political director in Texas, said weakness at the top of the ticket was hurting its prospects. "Certainly we had the chance for a blowout. If a Ronald Reagan had been on the ballot for us, we maybe could have picked up seven or eight seats."

With Democrats expected to make congressional gains in the Northeast, West and Midwest, Republicans need to seize "open" seats being vacated by retiring Democrats across the South, which has moved steadily away from Democrats in recent years.

Texas was a key part of that strategy and Republicans had hoped to win four of the six House seats being left open by Democrats. Two of the targets were in extremely conservative east Texas, which was a stronghold of die-hard Democrats dating all the way back to the era of Reconstruction but has seen solid Republican advances since the 1970s.

Now, however, Republicans virtually rule out victories there this time and are instead focusing on the 5th and 12th congressional districts in Dallas and Fort Worth, where John Bryant and Pete Geren, both Democrats, are retiring.

But Democrats and organised labour have their own targets and are spending lavishly in the Gulf coast district of Steve Stockman, a freshman Republican, in a bid to oust him. They also like their chances in another Gulf Coast district, where Republican incumbent Greg Laughlin, a former Democrat, lost his party's primary this year.

Democrats, humbled by years of steady reverses in a state where they once enjoyed a virtual monopoly, claim to have turned back the Republican tide by reassuring conservative voters. "We are addressing bread-and-butter things as opposed to divisive social issues like gays in the military, for example," said state Democratic Party chairman Bill White.

This year's Texas races were simultaneously thrown into chaos and given a pivotal role in the battle for the House when courts over the summer redrew 13 congressional districts. They acted after the Supreme Court ruled the Democratic-controlled state legislature had gerrymandered the boundaries of three districts on racial lines.

It immediately raised Republican hopes in several tight races, including the 5th District in Dallas where Republican candidate Pete Sessions was effectively given a boost of four percent, and the Houston district of Democratic incumbent Ken Bentsen, who now faces a battle to hold his seat.

By forcing annulment of primary election results in the 13 districts, the redrawing also made the Nov. 5 votes a free-for-all open to any number of candidates. With candidates needing 50 percent to win, some of those races will go to a second round in December.
If control of the House is still hanging in the balance after Nov. 5, the Texas runoffs will draw the attention of every politician, pundit and interest group in the country.
Republicans say their chances of picking up more seats in Texas are stronger in a second round of voting. "The more there are, the better it would be for us," Pauken said.
